About this document

  • This document describes the ClearML platform deployed with Dell AI Factory. Its purpose is to explain what the solution does, how it is structured, and how it is deployed and operated on Dell Technologies infrastructure. The emphasis is on concrete capabilities and operational clarity.

    The guide walks through the solution scope, core architecture, deployment model, security considerations, sizing guidance, and support boundaries. It is intended to support evaluation and implementation decisions, as well as day‑to‑day operation of ClearML as part of an enterprise AI factory.

Additional prerequisites

    • A local HTTP Server (such as Nginx, Apache, or S3-compatible storage) to host binaries.
    • A local Container Registry (for example, Harbor, Artifactory) to host container images and Helm charts (as OCI artifacts). See Appendix C for more details.

    Once the requirements are met, the following artifacts need to be mirrored locally.

    • Binaries: Mirror the Helm binary tarball to your local HTTP server.
      1. Download the required binaries on a machine with Internet access. Source: https://get.helm.sh/helm-v3.18.4-linux-amd64.tar.gz.
        #Download the Helm Binary (On a Machine With Internet)
        wget https://get.helm.sh/helm-v3.18.4-linux-amd64.tar.gz
      2. Upload them to your local HTTP server. Local Destination: http://<your-http-server>/helm-v3.18.4-linux-amd64.tar.gz.
        #On disconnected machine
        scp helm-v3.18.4-linux-amd64.tar.gz ser@ip_adress:/</home/user>/
        sudo mv /<home/user>/helm-v3.18.4-linux-amd64.tar.gz /var/www/html/helm-binary/
      3. Ensure the HTTP URL is reachable from the cluster/blueprint execution environment
    • Helm charts: ClearML Helm charts should be downloaded and pushed to your local Container registry as OCI artifacts.
      1. Log in to the Enterprise ClearML registry using your provided credentials: 
        helm registry login docker.io --username $YOUR_USERNAME --password $YOUR_PASSWORD
      2. Pull the following required components and versions using the OCI syntax below: 
        helm pull oci://docker.io/clearml/clearml-enterprise --version 10.11.15
         helm pull oci://docker.io/clearml/clearml-enterprise-agent --version 6.11.2
         helm pull oci://docker.io/clearml/clearml-enterprise-app-gateway --version 3.0.6
      3. Push the charts to your local registry. Choose a repository path (use lowercase, no underscores). For a plain container registry: 
        helm registry login <ip_addess>:5000 --username username1 --password password1
        helm push ./clearml-enterprise-10.11.15.tgz oci://172.16.44.54:5000/clearml
        helm push ./clearml-enterprise-agent-6.11.2.tgz oci://172.16.44.54:5000/clearml
        helm push ./clearml-enterprise-app-gateway-3.0.6.tgz oci://172.16.44.54:5000/clearml
        Note: Helm will derive the chart name and version from the package's Chart.yaml, creating the OCI reference: oci://<your-registry>/clearml/clearml-enterprise-agent:6.11.2.

      4. Confirm the list of charts uploaded to the registry:
        curl -u username1:password1 http://<ip_address>:5000/v2/_catalog
    • Container images: Identify and mirror all required container images to your local registry.
      1. Install Skopeo:
        sudo apt update
        sudo apt install -y skopeo
      2. Create file mirror_img.sh:
        #!/usr/bin/env bash
        set -euo pipefail

        LOCAL_REG="${LOCAL_REGISTRY:-}"
        SRC_USER="${DOCKER_IO_USERNAME:-}"
        SRC_PASS="${DOCKER_IO_PASSWORD:-}"
        DST_USER="${LOCAL_USER:-jarvis}"
        DST_PASS="${LOCAL_PASS:-jarvis}"

        if [[ -z "$LOCAL_REG" ]]; then
          echo "ERROR: LOCAL_REGISTRY is not set"
          exit 1
        fi

        IMAGES=(
          # Helm chart OCI artifacts
          "docker.io/clearml/clearml-enterprise:10.11.15"
          "docker.io/clearml/clearml-enterprise-agent:6.11.2"
          "docker.io/clearml/clearml-enterprise-app-gateway:3.0.6"

          # Container images
          "docker.dragonflydb.io/dragonflydb/dragonfly:v1.36.0"
          "docker.elastic.co/elasticsearch/elasticsearch:8.5.1"
          "docker.io/allegroai/clearml-enterprise-agent-k8s-base:1.30-1.9.0rc2-172"
          "docker.io/bitnamilegacy/mongodb:7.0.14-debian-12-r3"
          "docker.io/clearml/apiserver:3.28.6-627"
          "docker.io/clearml/fileserver:3.28.6-627"
          "docker.io/clearml/webserver:3.28.6-1709"
          "docker.io/clearml/ai-gateway-proxy:1.8.1"
          "docker.io/clearml/ai-gateway-router:2.14.0"
          "docker.io/clearml/clearml-enterprise-agent-k8s-base:1.30-2.0.8rc1-391"
          "docker.io/dtzar/helm-kubectl:3.19"
        )
        for SRC in "${IMAGES[@]}"; do
          # Strip registry to build destination path cleanly
          NAME_TAG="${SRC#*/}"        # e.g., clearml/apiserver:3.27.2-414
          DST="${LOCAL_REG}/${NAME_TAG}"
          echo "==> Copy ${SRC} -> ${DST}"

          skopeo copy \
            ${SRC_USER:+--src-creds "${SRC_USER}:${SRC_PASS}"} \
            --dest-creds "${DST_USER}:${DST_PASS}" \
            --dest-tls-verify=false \
            "docker://${SRC}" "docker://${DST}"
        done
      3. Make it executable:
        chmod +x mirror_img.sh
      4. Run the pull script:
        DOCKER_IO_USERNAME=allegroaienterprise
        DOCKER_IO_PASSWORD=dckr_XXXXXX

        LOCAL_REGISTRY_USER=jarvis
        LOCAL_REGISTRY_PASS=jarvis
        LOCAL_REGISTRY=${REGISTRY_IP}:5000

        ./mirror_img.sh
      5. Verify the cluster can pull from the local registry (containerd/docker trust + auth + TLS/HTTP rules as required).
      6. When deploying the blueprint in a disconnected environment, update the following inputs through the deployment UI.
    Table 7. Updates for inputs in disconnected environments
    Input Field Description Type State (M/O) Default
    Container Registry Credentials Secret

    The name of the secret containing credentials for the Container Registry to pull images.

    Action: The management worker pulls Helm charts from your local container registry using OCI.

    Create a DAPO secret of type Docker Configuration containing the credentials for your local registry.

    Provide the secret name in the Container Registry Credentials Secret input.

    		secret Mandatory n/a
    Software sources for ClearML

    The URL pointing towards your helm binary.

    Action: Update 'helm_binary_url' to provide the list of binaries and their local URLs.

    clearml_software_resources:

    helm_binary_url: https://<your-http-server>/helm-v3.18.4-linux-amd64.tar.gz

    		 string Optional https://get.helm.sh/helm-v3.18.4-linux-amd64.tar.gz
    Note: In a disconnected environment, only the ClearML Server blueprint requires disconnected-specific input configuration. The ClearML Tenant blueprint automatically inherits container registry, CA certificate, and Helm binary settings from the referenced Server deployment.

Audience

  • This guide is written for teams responsible for designing, deploying, and operating AI factories.

    It is relevant to IT and platform leaders who evaluate AI infrastructure and MLOps solutions and are accountable for scalability, security, and governance. It also addresses platform and infrastructure engineers who deploy and operate ClearML on Kubernetes and GPU‑accelerated Dell systems. Operational guidance is included for administrators responsible for access control, resource management, and ongoing maintenance within Dell AI Factory environments.

Business challenges

  • Enterprises moving beyond isolated experiments face a different class of AI problems. The challenge is no longer training a single model, but operating many concurrent AI workloads across teams, frameworks, and GPU resources in a controlled and repeatable way.

    Common obstacles include limited visibility into experiments and results, inconsistent environments that break reproducibility, and manual handoffs between development and operations that slow delivery. As GPU usage grows, teams struggle to allocate resources fairly, avoid idle capacity, and prevent contention between projects. Organizations that serve multiple independent entities on shared infrastructure face the additional challenge of enforcing complete isolation between tenants — ensuring that no data, experiments, credentials, or resources are visible across boundaries. These issues compound in on‑premises and regulated environments, where security, access control, and auditability are non‑negotiable.

    Without a unified control layer, organizations lack a consistent way to orchestrate training jobs, manage pipelines, track models and data lineage, and enforce operational policy across clusters. This leads to fragmented tooling, duplicated effort, and AI initiatives that stall before reaching production.

    Dell AI Factory provides the enterprise foundation for scalable, secure AI infrastructure. ClearML addresses the operational gap above that infrastructure by providing a single control plane for AI workloads. This enables organizations to move from ad hoc experimentation to governed, repeatable AI operations without introducing unnecessary complexity or sacrificing control.

Common issues

  • Table 9. Common issues
    Issue Solution
    External IP pending Check the cloud provider LoadBalancer quota, or use NodePort.
    404 errors Verify that the ingress host and path match. Check service exists.
    502/503 errors Backend pods are not ready. Check pod status and logs.
    TLS errors Verify that a certificate secret exists. Check the cert-manager logs.

Configuration Steps

  • If the need is confirmed in the pre-verification steps, proceed with the following configuration steps.

    1. Edit the CSI Isilon node DaemonSet. 
      kubectl edit daemonset <csi-isilon-node-daemonset> -n <csi-namespace>
    2. Locate the `spec.template.spec.tolerations` section.
    3. Add the following entry. 
      tolerations:
        # ... existing tolerations ...
        - key: "node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane"
          operator: "Exists"
          effect: "NoSchedule"

Connectivity

  • By default, ClearML uses Docker Hub as its primary container registry for images needed to run the ClearML. It also supports changing to a dedicated private container registry instead of Docker hub, if required.

    DNS must resolve the following required subdomains to the ingress entry point:

    • api.<BASE_DOMAIN>
    • app.<BASE_DOMAIN>
    • files.<BASE_DOMAIN>
    • agw.<BASE_DOMAIN> (Application Gateway)

    ClearML can be run in a fully unconnected environment. In unconnected deployments, container images and Helm charts are mirrored from public registries into a private container registry. During deployment, the DAPO Orchestrator ensures that all image references point to this private registry, enabling fully disconnected operation. Users must configure their Kubernetes cluster to trust and authenticate with the private container registry. For details, see Appendix B.

    • TLS
    • Ingress

Connectivity

  • TLS

    The ClearML application requires valid TLS certificates to operate in TLS mode. Certificates may be signed by a publicly trusted certificate authority or by a private certificate authority. ClearML expects the user to provide the CA certificate (ca.crt) as part of the deployment inputs. Certificate management can be handled using tools such as cert‑manager and trust‑manager, if needed. If needed, see Appendix E for detailed information about cert-manager and ClusterIssuer installation.

    Note: TLS setup is not required for the OpenShift environment.

Connectivity

  • Ingress

    Ingress in Kubernetes is an API object that manages external access to the services in a cluster, typically for HTTP(S). For the ingress resource to work, the cluster must have an ingress controller running. Cluster administrators are expected to select ingress controllers according to their requirements. ClearML is compatible with a wide range of ingress controllers. Nginx Ingress is a recommended option. See Appendix D for detailed instructions, if needed.

    Note: TLS setup is not required for the OpenShift environment.

    The ClearML Platform installation uses a cluster load balancer. A DNS CNAME record points to the load balancer. Then, that load balancer sends traffic to the nginx-ingress.

    For organizations that require an unconnected deployment, the ClearML solution can be implemented using the Dell Automation Platform. Please refer to Appendix B. To help you navigate this process with confidence, Dell Professional Services is available to provide guidance and execution support, ensuring a smooth and successful deployment.

    ClearML Platform exposes the following service endpoints:

    • 80/443 for HTTPS ingress traffic

Core architecture components

  • ClearML consists of three primary components that work together to provide a complete MLOps environment, as shown in Figure 3. The architecture is designed for Kubernetes-native deployment on Dell PowerEdge infrastructure with NVIDIA GPU acceleration.

    1. ClearML Control Plane: The ClearML Control Plane provides the backend services and the web-based user interface (UI). It serves as the central hub for experiment management, model registry, data management, and pipeline orchestration. The control plane manages all metadata, configurations, and user interactions.
    2. ClearML Agent: The ClearML Agent manages the orchestration of workloads on the Kubernetes cluster. It monitors task queues, provisions compute resources, schedules GPU workloads, and manages the life cycle of training jobs, inference endpoints, and pipeline steps.
    3. ClearML Application Gateway: The ClearML Application Gateway controls the networking, authentication, and authorization into and out of ClearML-provisioned pods. It provides secure ingress routing, TLS termination, and policy enforcement for all ClearML services and user-deployed applications.

    ClearML uses a two-blueprint deployment model to separate the server infrastructure from tenant environments. The ClearML Server blueprint deploys the Control Plane, which provides the API server, web interface, file server, and shared data services. The ClearML Tenant blueprint provisions individual tenant environments, each with a dedicated ClearML Agent and Application Gateway running in an isolated Kubernetes namespace. Each tenant operates as an independent organization with its own credentials, admin user, and API access — with no visibility into other tenants. This model allows a single ClearML Server to host multiple tenants, each deployed by running the Tenant blueprint once per tenant. Separate blueprints are available for Kubernetes and Red Hat OpenShift environments.

Dell Automation Platform

  • The Dell Automation Platform is a comprehensive infrastructure management and orchestration solution created to streamline and automate the deployment and life cycle management of your IT environments. It empowers your organization to move forward with confidence by simplifying how you manage infrastructure and workloads across private cloud, AI solutions, and edge environments. This unified platform gives you a consistent and scalable operational model, simplifying everything from initial deployment to ongoing management and freeing your teams to focus on innovation.

    Putting your solutions to work is made simpler with the platform's Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) approach, which provides a reliable and repeatable process for deploying workloads. This method reduces operational complexity and ensures consistent performance and governance across all your systems. By centralizing operations, the Dell Automation Platform helps you accelerate progress and get the most from your technology investments. It integrates smoothly with your existing enterprise systems, providing a solid foundation to deploy and manage powerful solutions, including advanced AI workloads, with greater speed and control.

    While this document focuses on deploying ClearML Platform with the Dell Automation Platform (DAP), Dell Technologies also provides the flexibility to deploy ClearML without DAP to suit different operational preferences. In addition, customers have the option to bring their own license to the Dell AI factory, enabling a deployment model that aligns with their unique needs and existing investments.

    ClearML uses a two-blueprint deployment model. The ClearML Server blueprint is deployed first to establish the shared platform infrastructure, including the API server, web interface, file server, and data services. The ClearML Tenant blueprint is then deployed once for each tenant to provision an isolated environment with its own compute agent and application gateway.

Deployment configuration options

  • The ClearML deployment uses two blueprints: the ClearML Server blueprint (deployed once per cluster) and the ClearML Tenant blueprint (deployed once per tenant). Each blueprint has its own set of configuration inputs, organized into the tables below.

    Table 5. ClearML Server blueprint configuration options
    # Input Field Description Type Required Default
    Target Kubernetes Cluster
    1 Target Kubernetes Type Select the target Kubernetes environment type. Choose AI for Dell AI-integrated clusters (labeled dellprivatecloudcluster in DAP). Choose External for any other cluster, including vanilla Kubernetes, RKE2, and OpenShift. string Yes —
    2 Target Kubernetes Deployment Deployment ID of the target Kubernetes cluster as registered in DAP. The dropdown filters automatically based on the Target Kubernetes Type selection. deployment_id Yes —
    3 Kubernetes Configuration Secret Secret name containing the kubeconfig file for accessing the target Kubernetes cluster. Created by DAP at the time of onboarding the cluster. secret_key Yes —
    ClearML Configuration
    4 Base Domain Base FQDN for all ClearML services. The blueprint creates subdomains: api.<base_domain>, app.<base_domain>, files.<base_domain>. The agw.<base_domain> subdomain is created by the Tenant blueprint. DNS must resolve all subdomains to the cluster LoadBalancer IP before deployment. Example: clearml.ai.lab. For OpenShift, fetch the base domain value using: oc get ingresscontroller default -n openshift-ingress-operator -o yaml and check the status.domain value. string Yes —
    5 Maximum Users Maximum number of users allowed in the ClearML Server instance across all tenants. integer Yes 10 (range: 1–1000)
    6 Portal Admin Credentials Secret Secret containing the initial admin username and password for the ClearML web portal. Secret type: Basic Authentication Credentials. Format: {"username": "<username>", "password": "<password>"} secret_key Yes —
    7 Authentication Cookie Name Cookie name used by ClearML authentication flows. Use the default value unless specific requirements exist. string Yes clearml-token-k8s
    8 API Credentials Secret Name DAP secret name where API credentials are stored after deployment. The blueprint automatically creates this secret with the generated API access key and secret key. string No clearml-api-credentials
    Storage Configuration
    9 Data Services Mode Select the data services deployment mode. bundled deploys MongoDB, Dragonfly (Redis-compatible), and Elasticsearch as part of the ClearML deployment. external uses pre-existing, customer-managed data services. string Yes bundled
    10 MongoDB Storage Class Kubernetes StorageClass for MongoDB persistent volumes. MongoDB requires a non-NFS storage backend such as block storage (for example, CSI PowerScale). Required when Data Services Mode is bundled. string Conditional —
    11 Dragonfly Storage Class Kubernetes StorageClass for Dragonfly (Redis-compatible) persistent volumes. NFS storage is acceptable. Required when Data Services Mode is bundled. string Conditional —
    12 Elasticsearch Storage Class Kubernetes StorageClass for Elasticsearch persistent volumes. NFS storage is acceptable. Required when Data Services Mode is bundled. string Conditional —
    13 FileServer Storage Class Kubernetes StorageClass for ClearML FileServer persistent volumes. NFS storage is acceptable. Required when Data Services Mode is bundled. string Conditional —
    14 MongoDB Storage Size Size of the persistent volume for MongoDB. Stores experiment metadata, project definitions, and user data. Increase for large-scale deployments. Required when Data Services Mode is bundled. string Conditional 50Gi
    15 Dragonfly Storage Size Size of the persistent volume for Dragonfly (Redis-compatible), the in-memory cache and message broker. Required when Data Services Mode is bundled. string Conditional 5Gi
    16 Elasticsearch Storage Size Size of the persistent volume for Elasticsearch, which powers search and log indexing. Scale proportionally with the number of experiments and log volume. Required when Data Services Mode is bundled. string Conditional 50Gi
    17 External MongoDB Connection Secret DAP secret (Raw/Opaque JSON) containing MongoDB connection details. Format: {"connection_string_auth": "mongodb://user:pass@host:port/auth_db", "connection_string_backend": "mongodb://user:pass@host:port/backend_db"}. Required when Data Services Mode is external. secret_key Conditional —
    18 External Dragonfly Connection Secret DAP secret (Raw/Opaque JSON) containing Dragonfly (Redis-compatible) connection details. Format: {"host": "dragonfly.example.com", "port": "6379", "password": "password", "tls": true}. Required when Data Services Mode is external. secret_key Conditional —
    19 External Elasticsearch Connection Secret DAP secret (Raw/Opaque JSON) containing Elasticsearch connection details. Format: {"host": "elasticsearch.example.com", "port": "9200", "scheme": "https", "username": "elastic", "password": "password"}. Required when Data Services Mode is external. secret_key Conditional —
    20 External CA Certificate Secret DAP secret (Raw/Opaque JSON) containing CA certificates for external services when using TLS. Format: {"ca_certificates": "-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----\n...\n-----END CERTIFICATE-----"}. Required when Data Services Mode is external and TLS is enabled. secret_key Conditional —
    Networking Configuration
    21 Ingress Class Name Name of the Kubernetes IngressClass used to expose ClearML services externally. The blueprint creates Ingress resources for api, app, and files subdomains. To find available IngressClasses: kubectl get ingressclasses. Common values: nginx, haproxy, traefik. string Yes —
    22 Cert Manager Cluster Issuer Name of a cert-manager ClusterIssuer that issues TLS certificates for all ClearML Ingress resources. Ensure the ClusterIssuer is in a Ready state before deploying. To list available issuers: kubectl get clusterissuers. string Yes —
    23 CA Certificate Secret Name of a DAP secret containing the CA certificate (ca.crt) used to sign ClearML server TLS certificates. The ClearML Agent and Application Gateway need this certificate to trust the ClearML API server over HTTPS. Secret type: General. secret_key Yes —
    Container Registry Configuration
    24 Container Image Registry Hostname or IP address of the container registry hosting ClearML images. Connected environments: keep the default docker.io. Disconnected environments: set this to your private registry address (for example, registry.local:5000). The blueprint automatically replaces docker.io in all image references and Helm chart OCI URLs with this value. string Yes docker.io
    25 Container Registry Credentials Secret Name of a DAP secret containing credentials for the container registry. Secret type: Docker Configuration. secret_key Yes —
    26 Secure Registry (HTTPS) Set to true for HTTPS registries (default). Set to false only for plain HTTP registries. boolean No TRUE
    27 Container Registry CA Certificate Name of a DAP secret containing the CA certificate for a private container registry. Required only if Secure Registry is true and using a private registry with a custom CA. Secret type: General. secret_key Conditional —
    Software Sources
    28 Helm Binary URL URL for downloading the Helm binary. In disconnected environments, point this to your internal HTTP file server. string No https://get.helm.sh/helm-v3.18.4-linux-amd64.tar.gz
    29 Helm Binary Checksum SHA256 checksum for the Helm binary archive. Used to verify the integrity of the downloaded file. string No f8180838c23d7c7d797b208861fecb591d9ce1690d8704ed1e4cb8e2add966c1
    Table 6. ClearML Tenant blueprint configuration options
    # Input Field Description Type Required Default
    ClearML Server Reference
    1 ClearML Server Deployment Deployment ID of the ClearML Server deployment to connect this tenant to. The dropdown automatically filters to show only ClearML Server deployments (labeled with solution: clearml_server). To find this value, navigate to Deployments in the DAP Orchestrator UI and locate your ClearML Server deployment. Cannot be changed after deployment. deployment_id Yes —
    Tenant Configuration
    2 Tenant Name Unique name for the tenant. Used for naming Kubernetes resources (namespaces, Helm releases, secrets). Must be 3–63 characters, lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens only. Cannot start or end with a hyphen. Examples: acme-corp, team-alpha, project123. Cannot be changed after deployment. string Yes —
    3 Tenant Admin Credentials Secret DAP secret containing the tenant admin user details. Secret type: Raw/Opaque (plaintext). Format: {"name": "John Doe", "email": "john.doe@example.com"}. The blueprint creates a ClearML company (tenant) and an admin user with the provided name and email. Cannot be changed after deployment. secret_key Yes —
    Agent Queue Configuration
    4 Agent Queue Configuration List of agent queue configurations for the tenant. Each queue entry requires a Queue Name (string) and optionally accepts CPU (string, for example 4 or 4000m), Memory (string, for example 32Gi or 512Mi), and GPU (string, for example 1). When empty (default), the ClearML Agent is deployed without queue mapping, and queues can be configured later through the ClearML UI. Cannot be changed after deployment — configure queues before deployment or modify later through the ClearML UI. list No (empty)

    Note: Dell Automation Platform offers several Dell Technologies-validated solution blueprints that Dell Technologies supports. However, Dell Technologies cannot support user-created blueprints or blueprints that a third party creates.

    CAUTION: Through blueprints, plug-ins, and/or other means (collectively, Blueprints), the Dell Automation Platform, may deploy and/or manage hardware, software, products, or services that are provided by a third-party manufacturer or supplier and are not Dell or Dell EMC branded (collectively, Third-Party Products). Notwithstanding any other provisions: (1) such Third-Party Products are subject to the standard license, services, warranty, indemnity, and support terms of the third-party manufacturer/supplier (or an applicable direct agreement between you and such manufacturer/supplier), to which you must adhere; (2) Blueprints are provided as is and without warranties or conditions; and (3) any warranty, damages, or indemnity claims against Dell in relation to such Third-Party Products and/or Blueprints are expressly disclaimed and excluded.
    1. On the Dell Automation Platform home tab, select Go to Catalog from the Catalog tile.
    2. On the Dell AI Solutions tile, click Explore Offers.

    6. Repeat these steps for both the Server and Tenant blueprints before proceeding.

    The downloaded blueprint now appears in the Dell Automation Platform Orchestrator under Inventory > Blueprints .

      Table 4. Secret details
      Secret Name Secret Type Sample Value Used By
      Portal admin credentials secret Basic Authentication Credentials

      username: admin

      password: password

      		 Server blueprint
      Container registry credentials secret Docker Configuration

      username: username

      password: password

      		 Server blueprint
      Tenant admin credentials secret Raw/Opaque {"name": "John Doe", "email": "john.doe@example.com"} Tenant blueprint

Deployment procedures

  • Deploy the ClearML Server blueprint

    Once all prerequisite steps are completed, deploy the ClearML Server to establish the shared platform infrastucture. The Server blueprint deploys the ClearML Enterprise Server with API, web UI, file server, and data services. It is deployed once per Kubernetes cluster.

    1. Navigate to Inventory > Blueprint in the DAP Orchestrator.
    2. In the list of available blueprints, select the ClearML Server blueprint for your platform (ClearML Server for Kubernetes or ClearML Server OpenShift for Red Hat OpenShift) and click Deploy.
    3. Enter a name for your deployment and click Next.
    4. In the Configuration section, provide the required inputs organized into the following categories, as shown in Figure 5:

      Target Kubernetes Cluster

      • Target Kubernetes Type: Select the target Kubernetes environment type. Choose AI when deploying to a Dell AI-integrated Kubernetes cluster. Choose External for any other Kubernetes cluster.
      • Target Kubernetes Deployment: The Deployment ID of the target Kubernetes cluster as registered in DAP. The dropdown filters automatically based on the Target Kubernetes Type selection.
      • Kubernetes Configuration Secret: The name of a DAP secret containing the kubeconfig file for accessing the target Kubernetes cluster. This secret is created by DAP at the time of onboarding the Kubernetes cluster.

      ClearML Configuration

      • Base Domain: The base fully qualified domain name (FQDN) for all ClearML services. The blueprint creates three service endpoints as subdomains of this domain: api.<base_domain>, app.<base_domain>, and files.<base_domain>. A fourth subdomain, agw.<base_domain>, is created when the first Tenant blueprint is deployed. DNS must be configured to resolve all subdomains to the cluster's LoadBalancer IP before deployment. Example: clearml.ai.lab.
      • Maximum Users: Maximum number of users allowed in the ClearML Server instance (default: 10, range: 1–1000). This setting controls multi-tenant capacity across all tenants.
      • Portal Admin Credentials Secret: The name of a DAP secret containing the initial admin username and password for the ClearML web portal. Secret type: Basic Authentication Credentials. After deployment, log in to the ClearML UI (https://app.<base_domain>) with these credentials.
      • Authentication Cookie Name: Cookie name used by ClearML authentication flows (default: clearml-token-k8s). Use the default value unless you have specific requirements.
      • API Credentials Secret Name: DAP secret name where API credentials will be stored after deployment (default: clearml-api-credentials). The blueprint automatically creates this secret with the generated API access key and secret key.

      Storage Configuration

      • Data Services Mode: Select the data services deployment mode. Choose bundled to deploy MongoDB, Dragonfly (Redis-compatible), and Elasticsearch as part of the ClearML deployment with persistent volumes. Choose external to use pre-existing, customer-managed data services. See Appendix H for deployment instructions and DAP secret formats for each external data service.

      When Data Services Mode is set to bundled, provide the following inputs:

      • MongoDB Storage Class: The Kubernetes StorageClass for MongoDB persistent volumes. MongoDB requires a non-NFS storage backend such as block storage (for example, CSI PowerScale).
      • Dragonfly Storage Class: The Kubernetes StorageClass for Dragonfly persistent volumes. NFS storage is acceptable.
      • Elasticsearch Storage Class: The Kubernetes StorageClass for Elasticsearch persistent volumes. NFS storage is acceptable.
      • FileServer Storage Class: The Kubernetes StorageClass for ClearML FileServer persistent volumes. NFS storage is acceptable.
      • MongoDB Storage Size: Size of the persistent volume for MongoDB (default: 50Gi). Stores experiment metadata, project definitions, and user data. Increase for large-scale deployments.
      • Dragonfly Storage Size: Size of the persistent volume for Dragonfly (default: 5Gi). The default is sufficient for most deployments.
      • Elasticsearch Storage Size: Size of the persistent volume for Elasticsearch (default: 50Gi). Scale proportionally with the number of experiments and log volume.

      When Data Services Mode is set to external, provide the following inputs instead:

      • External MongoDB Connection Secret: DAP secret (Raw/Opaque JSON) containing MongoDB connection details. Format: {"connection_string_auth": "mongodb://user:pass@host:port/auth_db", "connection_string_backend": "mongodb://user:pass@host:port/backend_db"}
      • External Redis/Dragonfly Connection Secret: DAP secret (Raw/Opaque JSON) containing Dragonfly connection details. Format: {"host": "dragonfly.example.com", "port": "6379", "password": "password", "tls": true}
      • External Elasticsearch Connection Secret: DAP secret (Raw/Opaque JSON) containing Elasticsearch connection details. Format: {"host": "elasticsearch.example.com", "port": "9200", "scheme": "https", "username": "elastic", "password": "password"}
      • External CA Certificate Secret: DAP secret (Raw/Opaque JSON) containing CA certificates for external services when using TLS. Format: {"ca_certificates": "-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----\n...\n-----END CERTIFICATE-----"}

      Networking Configuration

      • Ingress Class Name: The name of the Kubernetes IngressClass used to expose ClearML services externally. The blueprint creates Ingress resources for api, app, and files subdomains using this class. To find available IngressClasses: kubectl get ingressclasses. Common values: nginx, haproxy, traefik.
      • Cert Manager Cluster Issuer: The name of a cert-manager ClusterIssuer that issues TLS certificates for all ClearML Ingress resources. Each Ingress is annotated with this issuer so that cert-manager automatically provisions and renews certificates. Ensure the ClusterIssuer is in a Ready state before deploying.
      • CA Certificate Secret: The name of a DAP secret containing the CA certificate (ca.crt) used to sign the ClearML server TLS certificates. The ClearML Agent and Application Gateway need this certificate to trust the ClearML API server over HTTPS. Secret type: General.

      Container Registries

      • Container Image Registry: The hostname or IP address of the container registry hosting ClearML images. For connected environments, keep the default docker.io. For disconnected environments, set this to your private registry address (for example, registry.local:5000). The blueprint automatically replaces docker.io in all image references and Helm chart OCI URLs with this value.
      • Container Registry Credentials Secret: The name of a DAP secret containing credentials for the container registry. Secret type: Docker Configuration.
      • Secure Registry (HTTPS): Set to true for HTTPS registries (default). Set to false only for plain HTTP registries.
      • Container Registry CA Certificate: The name of a DAP secret containing the CA certificate for a private container registry. Required only if Secure Registry is true and using a private registry with a custom CA. Secret type: General.

      Software Sources

      • Helm Binary URL: URL for downloading the Helm binary (default: https://get.helm.sh/helm-v3.18.4-linux-amd64.tar.gz). In disconnected environments, point this to your internal HTTP file server.
      • Helm Binary Checksum: SHA256 checksum for the Helm binary archive (default: f8180838c23d7c7d797b208861fecb591d9ce1690d8704ed1e4cb8e2add966c1). Used to verify the integrity of the downloaded file.
    5. Click Next to review the configuration on the summary page.
    6. Click Deploy to begin the deployment process.
    7. From the Inventory > Deployments list, click the name of the deployment to view the deployment details.
    8. Select the Logs tab to view the deployment progress and related information. The blueprint executes the following steps in order:
      1. Input Validation — Validates all input parameters.
      2. Stack Verification — Verifies Kubernetes stack readiness (storage class, ingress controller, cert-manager).
      3. ClearML Server Deployment — Deploys ClearML Enterprise Server using Helm.
      4. Readiness Check — Verifies deployment readiness and service availability.
    9. Wait for the Server deployment to complete successfully before proceeding to the Tenant blueprint deployment. After successful deployment, the blueprint automatically generates API credentials and stores them in the DAP secret specified by the API Credentials Secret Name input.

Deployment procedures

  • Deploy the ClearML Tenant blueprint

    After the ClearML Server deployment completes successfully, deploy the ClearML Tenant blueprint to provision each tenant environment.

    1. Navigate to Inventory > Blueprint in the DAP Orchestrator.
    2. In the list of available blueprints, select the ClearML Tenant blueprint for your platform (ClearML Tenant for Kubernetes or ClearML Tenant OpenShift for Red Hat OpenShift) and click Deploy.
    3. Enter a name for your deployment and click Next.
    4. In the Configuration section, provide the required inputs organized into the following categories, as shown in Figure 6.

      ClearML Server Reference

      • ClearML Server Deployment: The Deployment ID of the ClearML Server deployment created in the previous step. The dropdown automatically filters to show only ClearML Server deployments. The blueprint automatically fetches all required configuration from the server deployment, including Kubernetes cluster details, ClearML API server URL, base domain, networking configuration, container registry settings, and CA certificates.

      Tenant Configuration

      • Tenant Name: A unique name for the tenant. This name is used for naming Kubernetes resources (namespaces, Helm releases, secrets) and must be unique across the ClearML Server instance. The tenant name must be 3–63 characters, lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens only. It cannot start or end with a hyphen. Examples: acme-corp, team-alpha, project123.
      • Tenant Admin Credentials Secret: The name of a DAP secret containing the tenant admin user details. Secret type: Raw/Opaque (plaintext). Format: {"name": "John Doe", "email": "john.doe@example.com"}. The blueprint creates a ClearML company (tenant) and an admin user with the provided name and email. Create this secret in Administration > Security > Secrets before deploying.

      Agent Queue Configuration

      • Agent Queue Configuration (optional): Define resource limits per queue. Each queue requires a name and optionally accepts CPU, memory, and GPU values. If left empty, the ClearML Agent is deployed without queue mapping, and queues can be configured later through the ClearML UI. See Appendix A for field details and examples.
    5. Click Next to review the configuration.
    6. Click Deploy to begin the deployment process.
    7. Monitor the deployment progress in the Logs tab. The blueprint executes the following steps in order:
      1. Input Validation — Validates tenant name, admin secret, and server deployment reference.
      2. Server Config Fetcher — Fetches configuration from the ClearML Server deployment (Kubernetes cluster, domain, registry, certificates).
      3. Tenant Provisioning — Creates the Kubernetes namespace, service account and RBAC roles, ClearML company (tenant), admin user, and API credentials (stored as DAP secrets).
      4. Agent Deployment — Deploys the ClearML Agent using Helm with the configured queues.
      5. Gateway Deployment — Deploys the ClearML Application Gateway using Helm with networking configuration.
      The blueprint provisions the following resources for each tenant:
      • A dedicated Kubernetes namespace
      • A ClearML company (tenant) with admin user and API credentials
      • A ClearML Agent deployment with configured queues
      • A ClearML Application Gateway deployment
    After successful deployment, the blueprint stores the tenant's API access key and API secret key as DAP secrets and returns the tenant admin user ID.

Executive summary

  • Enterprises are under pressure to move AI from experimentation into daily operations. Models are built faster than they can be governed, GPU resources are shared without clear control, and teams rely on fragmented tools that do not scale. The result is stalled projects, rising infrastructure costs, and limited trust in AI outcomes. What customers need is not more models, but a reliable way to operate AI as a repeatable, enterprise capability.

    ClearML on Dell AI Factory addresses this gap directly. Dell AI Factory provides the validated, GPU‑accelerated infrastructure required to run demanding AI workloads on‑premises and in regulated environments. ClearML adds the operational layer, acting as the control plane that governs how experiments, pipelines, models, and resources are tracked, run, and managed across teams. The platform supports multi-tenant operations, allowing multiple companies, teams, or business units to share infrastructure with full isolation and centralized governance. Together, they provide structure and visibility.

    In this solution, responsibilities are clearly defined. Dell delivers the compute, storage, networking, and life cycle support. NVIDIA GPUs provide acceleration. ClearML coordinates AI operations above the infrastructure, without forcing changes to existing frameworks, data platforms, or development workflows. Teams continue to work the way they do today, while ClearML enforces consistency, captures state, and provides control.

    This approach solves the problems customers face as AI adoption grows. Experiments become reproducible instead of disposable. Pipelines replace manual handoffs. GPU resources are shared with defined access and predictable usage. LLM workflows are managed with the same rigor as traditional models. Platform teams gain governance and visibility, while practitioners gain a stable environment to deliver results.

    ClearML on Dell AI Factory is designed for organizations ready to operationalize AI at scale. It provides the foundation to move from isolated success to sustained delivery, with clear ownership, controlled execution, and enterprise‑ready infrastructure. The next step is to align AI ambition with an operating model that can support it.

External Data Services Setup Reference

  • When deploying ClearML with the data services mode set to external, MongoDB, Dragonfly (Redis-compatible), and Elasticsearch must be deployed and accessible before the ClearML Server blueprint is deployed.

    The setup process is the same for all three services:

    1. Create a dedicated Kubernetes namespace for the service.

      For Kubernetes:

      kubectl create namespace <service-name>

      For OpenShift:

      oc new-project <service-name>

      Where <service-name> is mongodb, dragonfly, or elasticsearch.

    2. Deploy the service using Helm or the service operator (Non-TLS or TLS).
      Table 10. Deploy the service
      Service Method Non-TLS Install Command
      MongoDB Helm helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami && helm repo update && helm install mongodb bitnami/mongodb --namespace mongodb --set auth.enabled=true --set auth.rootPassword=<password> --set architecture=standalone --set persistence.enabled=true --set tls.enabled=false
      Dragonfly Operator kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dragonflydb/dragonfly-operator/main/manifests/dragonfly-operator.yaml then apply a Dragonfly custom resource with authentication and resource limits
      Elasticsearch Helm helm repo add elastic https://helm.elastic.co && helm repo update && helm install elasticsearch elastic/elasticsearch --namespace elasticsearch --set replicas=1 --set service.type=ClusterIP --set resources.requests.memory=1Gi --set resources.limits.memory=2Gi

      OpenShift modifications

      Add the following to the install commands when deploying on OpenShift:

      Table 11. OpenShift modifications
      Service Additional Parameters
      MongoDB Add --set podSecurityContext.enabled=false --set containerSecurityContext.enabled=false to the Helm install command
      Dragonfly Run oc adm policy add-scc-to-user privileged -z default -n dragonfly before deploying the Dragonfly custom resource
      Elasticsearch Run oc adm policy add-scc-to-user privileged -z default -n elasticsearch before the Helm install command

      TLS modifications

      Add or change the following when deploying with TLS:

      Table 12. TLS modifications
      Service Additional Parameters
      MongoDB Add --set tls.enabled=true --set tls.autoGenerated=true --set tls.mTLS.enabled=false --set 'extraFlags[0]=--tlsCAFile=/certs/mongodb-ca-cert' --set 'extraFlags[1]=--tlsAllowConnectionsWithoutCertificates'
      Dragonfly (k8s) Create a cert-manager Issuer and Certificate in the dragonfly-tls namespace, then deploy the Dragonfly custom resource with tlsSecretRef pointing to the generated certificate secret
      Dragonfly (OpenShift) Deploy Dragonfly first without TLS, then annotate the service: oc annotate service dragonfly -n dragonfly-tls service.beta.openshift.io/serving-cert-secret-name=dragonfly-tls and patch the Dragonfly resource to add tlsSecretRef
      Elasticsearch Add --set security.enabled=true --set security.tls.enabled=true --set security.tls.selfSignedCert.enabled=true
    3. Verify the deployment (check pods and services). 
      kubectl get pods -n <service-name>
      kubectl get svc -n <service-name>
    4. Create a DAP secret.

      Navigate to Administration > Security > Secrets in the DAP Orchestrator. Create a new secret of type Raw/Opaque using the formats below.

      Table 13. DAP secret
      Service DAP Secret Format (Non-TLS) DAP Secret Format (TLS)
      MongoDB {"connection_string_auth": "mongodb://root:<password>@mongodb.mongodb.svc.cluster.local:27017/auth?authSource=admin", "connection_string_backend": "mongodb://root:<password>@mongodb.mongodb.svc.cluster.local:27017/backend?authSource=admin"} Same, append &tls=true to each connection string
      Dragonfly (Redis-compatible) {"host": "dragonfly.dragonfly.svc.cluster.local", "port": 6379, "password": "<password>"} Same, add "tls": true
      Elasticsearch {"host": "elasticsearch-master.elasticsearch.svc", "port": 9200, "scheme": "http"} {"host": "elasticsearch-master.elasticsearch.svc", "port": 9200, "scheme": "https", "username": "elastic", "password": "<password>"}

      TLS certificates

      When using TLS, extract the CA certificate from the service deployment and store it in the External CA Certificate Secret (see Appendix A, Table A-1, row 20). Example extraction commands:

      # MongoDB
      kubectl get secret mongodb-ca -n mongodb -o jsonpath='{.data.mongodb-ca-cert}' | base64 -d > /tmp/mongodb-ca.crt
      # Dragonfly
      kubectl get secret dragonfly-tls -n dragonfly-tls -o jsonpath='{.data.ca\.crt}' | base64 -d > /tmp/dragonfly-ca.crt
      # Elasticsearch
      kubectl get secret elasticsearch-master-certs -n elasticsearch -o jsonpath='{.data.ca\.crt}' | base64 -d > /tmp/elasticsearch-ca.crt

      For detailed step-by-step deployment instructions for each service, contact Dell Professional Services or see the ClearML Enterprise deployment documentation.

Installation steps

  • Perform the following steps:

    1. Add an NGINX Ingress Helm repository. 
      helm repo add ingress-nginx https://kubernetes.github.io/ingress-nginx
      helm repo update
    2. Install NGINX Ingress Controller. 
      helm install ingress-nginx ingress-nginx/ingress-nginx \
        --namespace ingress-nginx \
        --create-namespace \
        --set controller.service.type=LoadBalancer
    3. Verify the installation. 
      # Check pods are running
      kubectl get pods -n ingress-nginx

      # Expected output:
      # NAME                                        READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
      # ingress-nginx-controller-xxxxxxxxx-xxxxx   1/1     Running   0          1m

      # Check service and get external IP
      kubectl get svc -n ingress-nginx

      # Expected output:
      # NAME                                 TYPE           CLUSTER-IP     EXTERNAL-IP     PORT(S)                      AGE
      # ingress-nginx-controller             LoadBalancer   10.x.x.x       <EXTERNAL-IP>   80:30080/TCP,443:30443/TCP   1m

      # Wait for external IP if pending
      kubectl get svc -n ingress-nginx -w
    4. Update the DNS.
      1. After installation, update the DNS to point to the NGINX ingress external IP:
        Table 8. Update the DNS to point to the NGINX ingress external IP
        Base Domain Value External IP
        api.<BASE_DOMAIN> A <EXTERNAL_IP>
        app.<BASE_DOMAIN> A <EXTERNAL_IP>
        files.<BASE_DOMAIN> A <EXTERNAL_IP>

        For DAPO Agent Cluster (CoreDNS)

      2. Edit the CoreDNS ConfigMap in the DAPO cluster:
        kubectl edit configmap coredns -n kube-system
      3. Add a hosts block.
        <EXTERNAL_IP>  api.clearml.ai.lab
           <EXTERNAL_IP>  app.clearml.ai.lab
           <EXTERNAL_IP>  files.clearml.ai.lab
           fallthrough
        }
      4. Restart CoreDNS.
        kubectl rollout restart deployment coredns -n kube-system

Installation steps

  • Perform the following steps:

    1. Install cert-manager. 
      kubectl apply -f https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/releases/download/v1.18.4/cert-manager.yaml
    2. Verify the installation.

      Wait for the cert-manager pods to be ready:

      kubectl get pods -n cert-manager
      Expected output:
      NAME                                       READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
      cert-manager-xxxxxxxxxx-xxxxx              1/1     Running   0          1m
      cert-manager-cainjector-xxxxxxxxxx-xxxxx   1/1     Running   0          1m
      cert-manager-webhook-xxxxxxxxxx-xxxxx      1/1     Running   0          1m
    3. Create a Self-Signed ClusterIssuer. 
      kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
      apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
      kind: ClusterIssuer
      metadata:
        name: selfsigned-issuer
      spec:
        selfSigned: {}
      ---
      apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
      kind: Certificate
      metadata:
        name: my-selfsigned-ca
        namespace: cert-manager
      spec:
        isCA: true
        commonName: my-selfsigned-ca
        secretName: root-secret
        privateKey:
          algorithm: ECDSA
          size: 256
        issuerRef:
          name: selfsigned-issuer
          kind: ClusterIssuer
          group: cert-manager.io
      ---
      apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
      kind: ClusterIssuer
      metadata:
        name: my-ca-issuer
      spec:
        ca:
          secretName: root-secret
      EOF
    4. Verify the ClusterIssuer. 
      kubectl get clusterissuer
      NAME                READY   AGE
      my-ca-issuer        True    7d1h
      selfsigned-issuer   True    7d1h
    5. Create a CA certificate secret.
      In the DAP Orchestrator, browse to Administration > Security > Secrets and create a new “CA Certificate” secret with type “General” and value with the output of the following command: 
      kubectl get secret root-secret -n cert-manager -o jsonpath='{.data.ca\.crt}' | base64 -d

Installation steps

  • Perform the following steps:

    1. Add the official Helm repo for the chart. 
      helm repo add nfs-subdir-external-provisioner https://kubernetes-sigs.github.io/nfs-subdir-external-provisioner/
      helm repo update
    2. Install the Helm chart. 
      helm install nfs-provisioner nfs-subdir-external-provisioner/nfs-subdir-external-provisioner \
        --namespace nfs-provisioner \
        --create-namespace \
        --set nfs.server=<ip_address>\
        --set nfs.path=/srv/nfs/share \
        --set storageClass.name=nfs-storage \
        --set storageClass.reclaimPolicy=Retain
    3. Verify the StorageClass to confirm the new nfs-storage class appears and is marked as default (if desired) and Provisioner is k8s-sigs.io/nfs-subdir-external-provisioner. 
      kubectl get sc
    4. Check the provisioner pod and wait until it is running. 
      kubectl get pods -n nfs-provisioner
    5. Grant the required SCC.
      OpenShift requires additional privileges for pods accessing host mounts. Apply the ClusterRoleBinding below to bind the Helm-created ServiceAccount to the hostmount-anyuid SCC: 
      kubectl apply -f - << 'EOF'
      apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
      kind: ClusterRoleBinding
      metadata:
        name: nfs-provisioner-scc-binding
      roleRef:
        apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
        kind: ClusterRole
        name: system:openshift:scc:hostmount-anyuid
      subjects:
        - kind: ServiceAccount
          name: nfs-provisioner-nfs-subdir-external-provisioner
          namespace: nfs-provisioner
      EOF

  • Dell AI Factory


    PowerEdge servers

    The Dell PowerEdge XE7740 and XE7745 servers are engineered to accelerate performance and drive progress for your most demanding enterprise workloads. These servers provide a powerful foundation for AI and machine learning, with exceptional processing capabilities and ample memory to handle large datasets. By bringing together advanced compute and storage in a dense, efficient design, the XE7740 and XE7745 help you turn complex data into actionable insights, empowering your teams to achieve their goals with confidence and speed.

    Dell AI Factory deployments support CPU silicon diversity, allowing organizations to choose Intel or AMD processors based on workload characteristics, performance requirements, and standardization preferences.

    Dell PowerEdge R670 and R6715 servers are typically used for management and control‑plane roles, providing a compact platform for orchestration, scheduling, and platform services. For general compute and AI workloads, PowerEdge R770 and R7725 deliver a dual‑socket platform with accelerator‑enabled configurations, making them suitable for data processing, analytics, and AI services. PowerEdge R7715 offers a single‑socket alternative for similar use cases.

    PowerEdge XE7740 and XE7745 provide dense PCIe GPU platforms optimized for high-performance AI and data analytics. PowerEdge XE9780 represents an 8U system for SXM GPUs. Together, these platforms enable a tiered design that separates management, general compute, and high-density GPU execution within the same Dell AI Factory environment.


    NVIDIA GPUs

    The NVIDIA B300, H200, H100, RTX PRO 6000, RTX PRO 4500 GPUs support a broad range of AI and data analytics workloads. The B300, H200 and H100 are designed for large‑scale model training and inference, offering high throughput for compute‑intensive tasks. The RTX PRO 6000 and RTX PRO 4500 provide versatile acceleration for mixed workloads, including analytics, visualization, and inference. Together, these GPUs allow organizations to match performance characteristics to workload requirements across enterprise environments.


    PowerSwitch with Enterprise SONiC

    AI workloads require networks that can move large amounts of data quickly and consistently with low latency. Dell PowerSwitch with Enterprise SONiC, including the SN‑series switches, provide a high‑performance Ethernet fabric designed for these needs, supporting scalable and efficient data movement across compute nodes. SN-series switches can also use Cumulus OS.

    Features such as congestion management, adaptive routing, and RDMA over Converged Ethernet (RoCE) help optimize communication between GPUs and reduce delays during training and inference. Together, these capabilities provide a simple, reliable networking foundation for AI environments while maintaining the flexibility of open Ethernet standards.

    NVAIE

    NVIDIA AI Enterprise (NVAIE) is a secure, end-to-end software platform that empowers organizations to accelerate their AI journey from pilot to production. It provides a comprehensive suite of tools and frameworks, optimized and supported to run on common data center infrastructure, streamlining the development and deployment of AI applications. By offering compatibility with leading AI frameworks and simplifying complex workflows, NVAIE helps your teams harness the full potential of AI with greater confidence and efficiency. This powerful platform provides the stability and performance needed to build and scale data science and AI workloads, helping you turn innovative ideas into real-world progress.

Key components

  • ClearML platform

    ClearML provides the operational layer for managing AI workloads across their full life cycle. The platform standardizes how experiments are tracked, how pipelines are run, and how models and artifacts move from development into deployment. ClearML is model-agnostic and supports both native and third-party model frameworks. Organizations can train, fine-tune, and deploy models using any major ML framework (PyTorch, TensorFlow, Hugging Face, and so on). ClearML provides integrated support for model versioning, lineage tracking, and automated model packaging for deployment.

    As shown in Figure 2, ClearML is organized into three functional layers above the customer compute fabric. The Infrastructure Control Plane manages GPU resources, queues, scheduling, and access control across clusters. Above it, the AI Development Center supports experiment tracking, dataset and model management, and pipeline orchestration used by data science and ML engineering teams. The GenAI App Engine provides a managed way to deploy and expose applications and inference services, with ClearML handling routing, authentication, and life cycle management.

    This layered structure allows ClearML to operate as a unified control plane without replacing existing tools. Users continue to work with their preferred frameworks and environments, while ClearML records state, enforces policy, and coordinates execution. Running on Dell AI Factory, this architecture supports controlled, repeatable AI operations on enterprise infrastructure, with clear separation between user interaction, orchestration, and underlying compute.

Home > Tools & Resources > DevOps and Automation > Automation and ITOps > White Papers > Solution Guide—ClearML on Dell AI Factory > Option 1: HTTP Private Container Registry

Option 1: HTTP Private Container Registry

  • Perform the following steps:

    1. Install dependencies and create authentication. 
      sudo apt-get install apache2-utils -y
      sudo mkdir -p /opt/registry/auth
      sudo htpasswd -Bc /opt/registry/auth/htpasswd password1
      # Password: password1
    2. Start the Docker registry. 
      sudo docker run -d \
        --name registry \
        -p 5000:5000 \
        -v /opt/registry/data:/var/lib/registry \
        -v /opt/registry/auth:/auth \
        -e "REGISTRY_AUTH=htpasswd" \
        -e "REGISTRY_AUTH_HTPASSWD_REALM=Registry Realm" \
        -e "REGISTRY_AUTH_HTPASSWD_PATH=/auth/htpasswd" \
        registry:2
    3. Configure Docker for HTTP registry. 
      /etc/docker/daemon.json
      {
        "insecure-registries": ["<ip_address>:5000"]
      }
    4. Restart Docker. 
      sudo systemctl restart docker
      sudo systemctl status docker
    5. Run a Docker registry test. 
      sudo cat /opt/registry/auth/htpasswd
      docker info | grep -A3 "Insecure Registries"
      cat /etc/docker/daemon.json
      docker login <ip_address>:5000
    6. Configure containerd for HTTP registry.
      1. Create a registry config directory. 
        sudo mkdir -p /etc/containerd/certs.d/<ip_address>:5000
      2. Create the hosts.toml file. 
        hosts.toml
        sudo tee /etc/containerd/certs.d/<ip_address>\:\5000/hosts.toml >/dev/null <<'EOF'
        server = "http:// <ip_address>:5000"
        [host."http:// <ip_address>:5000"]
          capabilities = ["pull", "resolve"]
          plain_http = true
        EOF
      3. Restart containerd.
        sudo systemctl restart containerd
    7. Create the image pull secret. 
      kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred \
        --docker-server=<ip_address>:5000 \
        --docker-username=jarvis \
        --docker-password='jarvis' \
        --docker-email=dummy@dummy.com \
        -n default
    8. Create a file named ‘test-pod.yaml’. 
      apiVersion: v1
      kind: Pod
      metadata:
        name: test-registry
      spec:
        containers:
          - name: busybox
            image: <ip_address>:5000/busybox:latest
            command: ["sleep", "3600"]
        imagePullSecrets:
          - name: regcred
    9. Deploy a test pod. 
      kubectl apply -f test-pod.yaml
    10. Configure Helm for insecure registry.
      Note: Helm should be ≥ 3.14 to allow the Helm CLI to connect with insecure registry.

      Create the following file: ~/.config/helm/registry/config.json. 

      {
        "insecure": true,
        "insecure-skip-tls-verify": true,
        "hosts": {
          "<ip_address>:5000": {
            "scheme": "http",
            "insecure": true
          }
        }
      }
    11. Use the following inputs in your ClearML blueprint:
      • Container registry name = Registry IP address
      • Container Registry Credentials Secret
      • Container registry secure = false
      • Container Registry CA Cert = blank
    Note: These inputs apply to the ClearML Server blueprint only. The ClearML Tenant blueprint automatically inherits container registry settings from the referenced Server deployment.

Home > Tools & Resources > DevOps and Automation > Automation and ITOps > White Papers > Solution Guide—ClearML on Dell AI Factory > Option 2: HTTPS private container registry

Option 2: HTTPS private container registry

  • Perform the following steps:

    1. Prepare the host.
      Note: Set up the OpenShift registry on the same machine where OCP is running (jump host). 

      REGISTRY_IP=<IP_ADRESS>
      sudo mkdir -p /opt/registry/{data,auth,certs}
      sudo chown -R $USER:$USER /opt/registry
    2. Create a local CA + IP certificate. 
      cd ~/registry-setup
      openssl genrsa -out ca.key 4096
      openssl req -x509 -new -nodes -key ca.key -sha256 -days 3650 \
        -subj "/CN=openshift-registry-CA" -out ca.crt

      cat > registry-ip.conf <<EOF
      [ req ]
      prompt = no
      distinguished_name = dn
      req_extensions = v3_req
      [ dn ]
      CN = ${REGISTRY_IP}
      [ v3_req ]
      keyUsage = keyEncipherment,dataEncipherment
      extendedKeyUsage = serverAuth
      subjectAltName = @alt_names
      [ alt_names ]
      IP.1 = ${REGISTRY_IP}
      DNS.1 = registry.local
      EOF

      openssl genrsa -out registry.key 4096
      openssl req -new -key registry.key -out registry.csr -config registry-ip.conf
      openssl x509 -req -in registry.csr -CA ca.crt -CAkey ca.key -CAcreateserial \
        -out registry.crt -days 3650 -sha256 -extensions v3_req -extfile registry-ip.conf

      cp registry.crt registry.key /opt/registry/certs/
      cp ca.crt /opt/registry/certs/ca.crt
    3. Configure basic auth. 
      htpasswd -Bbc /opt/registry/auth/htpasswd jarvis jarvis
    4. Run the registry container. 
      podman run -d --name registry \
        -p 5000:5000 \
        -v /opt/registry/data:/var/lib/registry:Z \
        -v /opt/registry/auth:/auth:Z \
        -v /opt/registry/certs:/certs:Z \
        -e REGISTRY_HTTP_ADDR=0.0.0.0:5000 \
        -e REGISTRY_HTTP_TLS_CERTIFICATE=/certs/registry.crt \
        -e REGISTRY_HTTP_TLS_KEY=/certs/registry.key \
        -e REGISTRY_AUTH=htpasswd \
        -e REGISTRY_AUTH_HTPASSWD_REALM="Registry Realm" \
        -e REGISTRY_AUTH_HTPASSWD_PATH=/auth/htpasswd \
        registry:2
    5. Verify. 
      curl --cacert /opt/registry/certs/ca.crt -u jarvis:jarvis https://${REGISTRY_IP}:5000/v2/_catalog
    6. Trust the CA (must be run on all nodes). 
      #from jump host
      scp ~/registry-setup/ca.crt core@100.96.54.34:/tmp/registry-ca.crt

      #from Openshift node:
      sudo mkdir -p /etc/containers/certs.d/100.96.54.172:5000
      sudo cp /tmp/registry-ca.crt /etc/containers/certs.d/100.96.54.172:5000/ca.crt
      sudo cp /tmp/registry-ca.crt /etc/pki/ca-trust/source/anchors/registry-ca.crt
      sudo update-ca-trust
      sudo systemctl restart crio
    7. Configure a pull secret (on Openshift cluster). 
      kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred \
        --docker-server=100.96.54.172:5000 \
        --docker-username=jarvis \
        --docker-password='jarvis' \
        --docker-email=dummy@dummy.com \
        -n default
    8. Test the pull secret. 
      cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
      apiVersion: v1
      kind: Pod
      metadata:
        name: test-registry
      spec:
        containers:
        - name: busybox
          image: 100.96.54.172:5000/busybox:latest
          command: ["sleep", "3600"]
        imagePullSecrets:
        - name: regcred
      EOF
         ```
      #Verify
      kubectl describe pod test-registry -n default
    9. If needed, delete the following secrets so the blueprint can recreate them with the updated credentials: 
      oc delete secret clearml-input-validator-pull-secret -n default --ignore-not-found
      oc delete secret clearml-stack-verifier-pull-secret -n default --ignore-not-found
    10. Use the following inputs in the ClearML blueprint:
      • Container registry name: registry IP address
      • Container Registry Credentials Secret: registry secret name
      • Container registry secure = true
      • Container Registry CA Cert = secret with the content of ~/registry-setup/ca.crt
    Note: These inputs apply to the ClearML Server blueprint only. The ClearML Tenant blueprint automatically inherits container registry settings from the referenced Server deployment.

Customers must maintain an active vendor contract and vendor software administrative capability.

Post-deployment verification

  • Confirm ClearML Platform pod status

    Confirm that all ClearML Platform components are running Pod Status using DAP Orchestrator.

    1. Open the DAP Orchestrator.
    2. Navigate to  Inventory > Infrastructure.
    3. Select the cluster where the ClearML workload was deployed.
    4. Click the Pods tab.
    5. Ensure that all pods within the clearml namespace (Server components) are in a Running state. For each deployed tenant, verify that all pods within the tenant-specific namespace (named after the tenant) are also in a Running state. Tenant namespaces contain the ClearML Agent and Application Gateway pods for that tenant.

Post-deployment verification

  • Verify GPU resource visibility

    Confirm that the ClearML platform detects the expected GPU resources:

    1. Browse to the Dashboard or Orchestration view.
    2. Verify that the GPU count displayed matches the number of GPUs available in the Kubernetes cluster worker nodes.
    3. If GPU resources are not visible, check that the NVIDIA GPU Operator is running and that worker nodes have the correct GPU driver version installed.
      Note: Recommended version for Jupyter Lab application on ClearML: 1.17.3 or later.

Home > Tools & Resources > DevOps and Automation > Automation and ITOps > White Papers > Solution Guide—ClearML on Dell AI Factory > Pre-deployment tasks

Pre-deployment tasks

  • Target cluster prerequisites

    To ensure compatibility and optimal performance, the target Kubernetes cluster must meet the following requirements:

    • Supported platform: Confirm that the target platform is supported. See the offer blueprint description for detailed compatibility information.
    • Operating System: Ubuntu 24.04 or later for Kubernetes configuration or Red Hat OpenShift 4.20 or later.
    • NVIDIA GPU drivers: Nodes equipped with GPUs (typically worker nodes) must have NVIDIA GPU driver version 580.107.02 or higher installed.
    • CUDA toolkit: Ensure that CUDA version 13.0 compatible is installed on GPU-enabled nodes.
    • Kubernetes version: The cluster must be running Kubernetes version 1.34 or later.
    • NVIDIA GPU operator: This operator must be deployed on the cluster to manage GPU resources.
    • Cluster inventory: The target cluster must be added to the inventory using DAPO.
    • External load balancer: Organizations are recommended to install a load balancer, such as MetalLB, to enable load balancing capabilities and configure with a public IP address pool.
    • Ingress controller: An ingress controller, such as NGINX-ingress, is required for access to the front-end services of ClearML.
      Note: Ingress setup is not required for the OpenShift environment.

    • Cert-manager: Certificate-manager and trust-manager must be installed to manage internal and external-facing certificates.
      Note: TLS setup is not required for the OpenShift environment.

    • Storage class: Storage classes must be configured and enabled within the Kubernetes cluster.

      ClearML requires separate storage classes for each data service. MongoDB requires a non-NFS storage backend such as block storage (for example, CSI PowerScale). Dragonfly (Redis-compatible), Elasticsearch, and FileServer can use NFS storage. See Appendix A for the full list of storage inputs.

      Note: For Red Hat OpenShift configuration, additional configuration steps are required to set up a storage class. See Appendix G for more details.

    • DNS configuration: All required subdomains must resolve to the ingress entry point before deployment. ClearML requires four subdomains: api.<BASE_DOMAIN>, app.<BASE_DOMAIN>, files.<BASE_DOMAIN>, and agw.<BASE_DOMAIN>. See Appendix D for DNS configuration details.
    • Kubernetes deploying user permissions: The Kubernetes deploying user permissions listed above are required for the ClearML blueprint deployment. These permissions are necessary for the DAP Orchestrator to create the Kubernetes resources that ClearML requires. Organizations should ensure the deploying service account or user has these permissions on the target cluster before initiating the blueprint deployment.
      • Create and bind Role and ClusterRole objects
      • Create ServiceAccounts, Secrets, and ConfigMaps
      • Create Deployments, Jobs, DaemonSets, and PodDisruptionBudgets

Home > Tools & Resources > DevOps and Automation > Automation and ITOps > White Papers > Solution Guide—ClearML on Dell AI Factory > Pre-verification steps

Pre-verification steps

  • Perform the following steps:

    1. Identify the CSI Namespace and DaemonSet. 
      # List all DaemonSets across namespaces to find the CSI Isilon node DaemonSet
      kubectl get daemonsets -A | grep -i isilon
      Expected output example: 
      csi-isilon csi-isilon-node 2 2 1 1 1 5d

      Note the “namespace” and “DaemonSet name” from the output.

    2. Verify that the CSI pods are not running on the control plane node. 
      # List CSI pods with node information
      kubectl get pods -n <csi-namespace> -o wide

      Check if any CSI node pod is running on the control plane node. If not, this confirms the need for the additional configuration steps.

    3. Check current tolerations on the DaemonSet. 
      kubectl describe daemonset <csi-isilon-node-daemonset> -n <csi-namespace> | grep -A 15 "Tolerations"

      If the output does not include “node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane”, the DaemonSet lacks the required toleration.

    4. Confirm that the pods remain unavailable due to volume related causes. 
      # Check PVC status
      kubectl get pvc -n <application-namespace>

      # Check pod events for volume errors
      kubectl describe pod <stuck-pod-name> -n <application-namespace> | tail -30

      Look for events like:

      • `FailedAttachVolume`
      • `FailedMount`
      • `WaitingForFirstConsumer`

Security and access control

  • Dell believes that trust is the foundation of progress, which is why security is at the core of this powerful solution. To protect your most valuable asset, your data, this solution employs a zero-trust security framework that safeguards information at every turn. All data is protected with robust encryption, both while at rest and in transit, ensuring it remains secure across your entire ecosystem. This solution is designed to support your data sovereignty needs and is built to adhere to the highest global standards, giving you the confidence to innovate while maintaining compliance. By default, cert-manager can manage the deployment and life cycle of certificates.

    Cert-manager automatically issues, renews, and rotates TLS certificates within the cluster with zero downtime.

    When configured, TLS certificates will be generated at deploy time for clients and servers, stored as secrets in Kubernetes and mounted into each service's containers. The CA certificate used for signing these keys will be provided and configured to support both Public CA and Private CA use cases.

    Empowering your teams with AI requires a system that you can manage with precision and clarity. Granular, role-based access controls allow you to define exactly who can use specific tools, data, and AI agents, ensuring the right people have the right permissions. The platform provides complete visibility into system operations through detailed audit logs, creating a clear record of all activities for monitoring and verification. With flexible deployment options, including on-premises or unconnected environments, you have complete control over where your data lives, allowing you to put powerful AI to work securely and responsibly.

    • General security considerations
    • ClearML platform security
    • Monitoring and observability

Security and access control

  • General security considerations

    AI solutions exist at the intersection of rapidly evolving AI technology and the ever-challenging security landscape. This unique position brings both incredible opportunities and significant risks. The security of any system exists in relation to the system’s threat profile: the value of a system's assets, the likelihood of an attempted attack, and the nature of potential attackers in terms of their resources, capabilities, and incentives. Furthermore, there is often a tension between security and convenience. Extra security measures might interfere with desirable use cases or lead to false-positive results. Therefore, Dell Technologies advises customers and architects to consider their specific operational contexts and conduct appropriate analysis to validate the applicability of the recommendations in this guide. Depending on the threat profile, additional services and security measures might be advisable.

    Note that the recommendations in the security best practices guide are not a complete security evaluation of the Dell AI Factory in its entirety or its individual components, nor a complete threat and risk analysis. You can also find additional information at the Dell Security and Trust Center.

    ClearML emphasizes robust security measures to protect enterprise data and ensure compliance with global standards. Their platform incorporates multi-layered protection, including encryption at rest and in transit, customizable data handling, and private deployment. For more detailed information, you can explore their Security Page, which provide insights into their security protocols, certifications, and compliance resources.

Security and access control

  • ClearML platform security

    ClearML implements a workspace-based access control model that governs permissions at multiple levels across the platform. Workspaces provide logical isolation within a tenant, each containing its own resources, experiments, models, datasets, and pipelines. Within each workspace, administrators define user roles controlling read, write, and run permissions across platform resources. ClearML enforces compute, network, and data isolation between tenants at the Kubernetes namespace level, with application-layer controls preventing cross-tenant access to experiments, models, or artifacts. Each tenant is provisioned as a fully independent organization with its own dedicated Kubernetes namespace, compute agents, application gateway, API credentials, and administrative controls. Tenant administrators manage their own users and permissions without visibility into other tenants.

    Built on this foundation, ClearML embeds enterprise security into every layer of the AI platform stack - from identity to inference.

    • Identity and access Control: The platform integrates directly with your existing Identity Provider using SAML 2.0, OIDC, or LDAP for single sign-on, syncing users and groups automatically to enforce fine-grained, project-level access control across experiments, models, datasets, and GPU worker queues.
    • Service accounts and automation security: Automated workloads, agents, CI/CD pipelines, and scheduled jobs authenticate through dedicated service accounts with API credentials, purpose-built for machines. Service accounts are governed by the same group memberships, access rules, and administrator vaults as human users, and support impersonation so agents can perform tasks on behalf of specific users while maintaining a full audit trail.
    • Configuration governance: Administrator Vaults give your IT and security teams centralized enforcement over the full runtime profile for platform teams—covering credential and secrets management, environment variable injection, runtime configuration files, storage destinations and storage credentials, default container images with match rules and override controls, Git and API token management, and platform-wide settings including logging, networking, and package management. Credentials are layered across admin, group, and user levels, and in unconnected environments the vault can redirect all dependencies to internal mirrors.
    • Compute governance: GPU Resource pools, quotas, and reservations ensure no team can overconsume while production workloads maintain guaranteed capacity.
    • Model serving and application security: The AI Application Gateway acts as the secure front door for all externally accessible workloads—not just model endpoints, but also NVIDIA NIM containers, remote development environments like VS Code, Jupyter Lab, and SSH sessions and any custom container launched through the platform. Every request requires token authentication with configurable expiration and instant revocation, RBAC scoped to group membership controls who can reach which endpoint, and all traffic is SSL-secured. Static routes provide stable, consumer-facing URLs that decouple the endpoint address from the model instance behind it—enabling redeployment, model swaps, canary deployments, and load balancing. Full model lineage traceability and Kubernetes network and namespace isolation between serving and training workloads round out the production security posture.
    • Audit and compliance: Task-level audit trails, automatic credential redaction, and Prometheus integration make the entire chain provable to auditors and regulators. All authentication events, configuration changes, and resource access are captured, providing the trail required for compliance reporting.
